title: Web Crawler
summary: Design a crawler that discovers and downloads billions of pages politely, without duplicates or traps.
statement: Design a distributed web crawler for a search engine. It starts from seed URLs, fetches pages, extracts links, and repeats, while respecting robots.txt and per-site rate limits, avoiding duplicates, and keeping content fresh. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Avoid duplicate pages and crawler traps.
Recrawl pages to keep content fresh.

requirementQuestions.question: How many pages must be crawled per second and in total?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: Is the crawl broad or focused, and which content types are included?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: How fresh must pages be and how often are important sites recrawled?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: How do you stay polite and avoid being blocked?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Adds validation, rate limiting, and fraud controls to the critical path.

requirementQuestions.question: How is fetched content stored and handed to indexing?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

requirementQuestions.question: How are failures and slow sites handled?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: What bandwidth and storage does the crawl need?
How many URLs sit in the frontier?
How many distinct hosts exist and how many fetchers are needed?

keyDecisions.question: How are URLs queued and prioritised?
considerations: Priority queues by importance and freshness.
Partition the frontier by host hash.

keyDecisions.question: How are duplicates avoided?
considerations: URL normalisation and a seen-URL set (Bloom filter or sharded store).
Trap detection by depth and pattern limits.

keyDecisions.question: How is each site protected?
considerations: One connection per host at a time.
Adaptive rates based on response times.

keyDecisions.question: Where does content go?
considerations: Raw pages to distributed object storage.

tradeoffs.tension: More frequent recrawls use more bandwidth and annoy sites.
Memory versus false positives that skip pages.

commonMistakes: Hammering a single host with parallel requests.
No URL normalisation, so duplicates multiply.
Falling into infinite calendar or session-ID traps.
followUps: How do you crawl JavaScript-heavy pages?
How do you detect when a page has changed?
How do you prioritise newly discovered high-quality sites?
How do you distribute the crawl across regions?
